utterances.text: Well, Koprivnica is in northern Croatia, near Zagreb. It's about 400 kilometres away from the Dubrovnik area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you have any information about the fact that other volunteers came in from other parts of Croatia and broke through to the Dubrovnik region in order to set up resistance to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Volunteers did come forward, mostly from Western Herzegovina but also from other parts of Croatia while you could still access Dubrovnik, as well as on the ship called "SLAVIJA," the one you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know, roughly speaking, how many such volunteers there were from the "SLAVIJA" vessel who managed with the help of President Mesic to reach Dubrovnik, to enter Dubrovnik, at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kos told me at the time that after the speech delivered by President Mesic on the ship, 45 volunteers came forward, and they were issued weapons and sent to the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps ask Damir Kos who issued them weapons, who distributed the weapons to them?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and he explained that they were given weapons, as he said, from the building he indicated. And I knew that to be the headquarters of the Territorial Defence of Dubrovnik, while that particular command was still in existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, where the building of the command and headquarters of the Dubrovnik Territorial Defence was in fact located. Give us a closer idea.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember. I can't actually locate it, but before the war everybody knew where the TO headquarters for Dubrovnik were and where they had their weapons stored. I think the Croatian National Guards' Corps was put up there, too, during the Dubrovnik operation, or the so-called Dubrovnik operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And can you tell me how you came to know that that was where the Croatian National Guards' Corps was put up, how did you come by that piece of information?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were -- it was intelligence that we learnt and also information from refugees and officers who had fled Dubrovnik. And I was also told, I think, by Kos himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did he happen to tell you whether those 45 volunteers, all armed and sent to the front lines of defence of Dubrovnik, whether they were all sent there?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I've said already.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, did you yourself during your command of the 9th Military Naval Sector in the period between October and December 1991 have under your command any paramilitaries, paramilitary formations?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me, please, whether the units of the 9th Military Naval Sector took control of Cavtat.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you recall the date when that happened?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the 16th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You as the commander, did you take the decision to implement that assignment?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Although I didn't enter with any combat troops and there was no combat or fighting or any damages at all in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, was Cavtat taken control of by only the units of the 9th Military Naval Sector, or did the units of the 2nd Tactical Group take part in that operation as well?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think there was a detachment of the 3rd Battalion, a company of the 3rd Battalion there, that they took part, but without entering the town, just along the access roads into town without any fighting. And I demanded that they should refrain from opening fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What about General Stankovic, was he in command of the 2nd Tactical Group at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were you given any resistance when you tried to enter Cavtat?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we weren't met with any resistance. Somebody just shot a projectile from a hunting rifle. Some individual from Cavtat shot from a hunting rifle. That was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, the units of the 9th Military Naval Sector, did they then assume control of Cavtat?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It was in our zone, our area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And how did you regulate life and work in the town of Cavtat itself? Did the local inhabitants stay on?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Nobody was evacuated from Cavtat of the local inhabitants. They remained. And under such conditions, life went on without any major restrictions or disturbances. And I remember that I even allowed people to fish in the sea somewhat later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, tell me this, please: The units under your command, did they also assume control of Mali and Veliki Zaton?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, when this happened, what time period, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was after the fall of Mokosica, which would make it towards the end of November. Veliki and Mali Zaton were taken control of without any fighting; everything was done peacefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And did you take control of Mokosica?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We entered Mokosica without any combat, thanks to the negotiations that had taken place with Minister Bernard Kouchner.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to remember what period of time that was, when that happened?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was on the 19th or 20th or 21st of November. That's when we entered Mokosica together, and a small quantity of weapons were surrendered to us by the inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, since you've said that you entered Mokosica together with Bernard Kouchner, whether before that you had any communication with him and if so what type and to what extent before entering Mokosica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. The evidence is not that he entered with Bernard Kouchner. There's no indication that Bernard Kouchner occupied Mokosica.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Perhaps I didn't understand what the witness said, but I will restate my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did Bernard Kouchner enter Mokosica at all together with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to explain, Your Honour, with the Court's indulgence. Before entering Mokosica, negotiations were held that there should be no fighting or combat and shooting around town, so that there were no injuries or casualties which had happened in October and to a certain extent at the start of November. And on behalf of the 2nd Operational Group these negotiations were conducted by Colonel Damjanovic. And he was promoted to the rank of general subsequently. And I joined the team, the group, later on and we demanded that weapons should be surrendered and that the units should enter without any fighting. Now, after these negotiations that is what actually happened, but we lost a soldier on the occasion. One of our soldiers were killed because somebody shot from an ambush, from a rifle, killing this one soldier. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And did you enter at the same time as Ben Kouchner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Before entering Mokosica with Bernard Kouchner, could you tell us, please, how many days before entering were those negotiations held and the contacts you had, the ones you mentioned a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't say for sure, but the negotiations went on for several days and the negotiations were led by -- or conducted by Colonel Svicevic on behalf of the 2nd Operational Group. And I think I think the negotiations were held in Cavtat. And that also taking part was a representative of the European Community. Whether it was Mr. Di Mistura, I'm not quite sure, but the negotiations did go on for several days. And they were perhaps continued after Mokosica, but I did not take part in them after that stage, so I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In those negotiations was the Dubrovnik side represented at all?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a representative of the Crisis Staff taking part, a man who always took part at negotiations -- or rather, there were two gentlemen who always took part. They would always be present at negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to remember a name? Can you give us a name?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of them was called Kolic, and he was a civilian. And the other man was an officer. He wore camouflage uniform, but I've forgotten his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did Nikola Obuljen perhaps take part in those negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He may have. I don't remember him specifically, but he had certainly taken part in the previous round of negotiations. He may have taken part in these as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know if those negotiations resulted in any specific agreement, if any document was signed, if there was an agreement between the parties?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I can answer that question. I know that the area surrounding Mokosica, because that was the area where I was involved, where my units were involved, we tried to prevent combat from breaking out. The negotiations took quite a while. And I'm not sure if any document was signed eventually. Colonel Svicevic was directly subordinated to General Strugar. He was the head of the negotiations team -- the negotiating team, and he reported to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Very well. What about your units? Did they take Zupa Dubrovacka?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did, with the exception of a few villages just underneath the main road. But they did take control of all the other sections of Zupa.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the specific time period in which this happened?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was on the 24th and 25th -- actually, it was on the 24th. There was no actual fighting going on really --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, of what month? Of what month? 24th? 25th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] October. There was no fighting in or around Zupa. After the landing at Kupari the paramilitary units had withdrawn from Zupa and the 3rd and 4th Battalions had taken control of some villages in their previous operations, some hamlets just next to the main road. Therefore, there was no major fighting on that occasion or destruction in the villages of Zupa Dubrovacka.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: It goes without saying that all the days we have been referring to relate to the year of 1991. Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The units under your command, did they take control of Kupari, too?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did. We landed at Kupari on the 24th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just a small correction. He said: "I landed at Kupari." And the interpretation reads: "We landed at Kupari."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The occupation of Kupari took place on the same day that Zupa Dubrovacka was taken, or is there a difference in terms of time?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 23rd and 24th of October was when the units of the 472nd Brigade that were on the left flank of the combat deployment of the brigade, meaning the 3rd and 4th Battalions, in their operations they crushed the defence along the main focal points along the Trebinje/Dubrovnik road, along the main strongholds along the Trebinje/Dubrovnik road. So that once my units reached Zupa after the landing, there were no defenders left there. They had pulled out taking small paths and the main road across to Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So first you took control of Kupari, and then you reached Zupa Dubrovacka the way you've just explained. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was there any fighting around Kupari, the taking of Kupari itself?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Two artillery weapons were firing from Kupari, and those were damaging us. My idea was by assault, by a small scale landing, to take over the command that was located at Kupari and to crush the defending unit and to practically bring the operation to an end, at least as far as my side was concerned, the south-east of Dubrovnik. There was sudden fighting that broke out. They were not expecting us, so the whole thing took a very brief while and we suffered no losses at all. I believe the enemy's casualties were very small also.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you have any artillery support during that particular attack?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was support from the artillery. They were firing. On their weapons -- we were trying to neutralise their weapons, and yet we tried to avoid hitting any of the hotels from land or sea during that operation. But there was damage that was done to the hotels nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us who support -- who provided artillery support from land and from sea.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were three patrol boats from the sea and the support from the land came, I think, from a battery of 130-millimetre and 85-millimetre weapons. Probably the artillery weapons from Prevlaka, too, were involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it has been omitted in the interpretation. "My artillery" is what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you be more specific about the location where the battery of 130- and 85-millimetre guns was deployed?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they were somewhere between Gruda and the Cilipi airport. The distance was between 8 and 10 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: This distance between 8 and 10 kilometres between the battery and?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between the battery and the Kupari area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The units under your command, did they take control of Dubac?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the 3rd Battalion of the 5th Brigade. That was the only infantry unit that I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What about the specific time period?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 24th and 25th, the same day after the landing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So we're talking about October 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, those operations around Kupari, Zupa Dubrovacka, and Dubac were connected, weren't they, at least in terms of the time period, the time frame?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was an operation that was planned and ordered by the command of the 2nd Operational Group. Taking part in this operation, there was some elements of my sector and elements of the 472nd Brigade. Artillery fire was coordinated and ordered in terms of specific tasks by Colonel Petkovic, who was the chief of the 2nd Artillery Group. There was a proposal for the use of artillery that was adopted by the command of the 2nd Operational Group, and I received this document and told to carry it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is that the proposed use of artillery that we talked about during the examination-in-chief that was signed by Petkovic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In the 9th VPS, did you have your own assistant or chief of artillery?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a chief of artillery, Lieutenant Colonel Anto Cirjak, one of the few officers, superior officers of Croatian nationality who stayed with the forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In line with the proposals by Petkovic from the 2nd Operational Group, did he control the use of artillery at the disposal of the 9th VPS?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The units under your command, did they take control of Zarkovica as well?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zarkovica was taken by the 4th Battalion of the 472nd Brigade on the 25th. There was no fighting. They simply took over a position that had been abandoned by the Croatian forces, and there was no fighting whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I forgot to ask you about Dubac, when Dubac was taken by the 3rd Battalion of the 5th Brigade, was there any artillery fire in terms of artillery support there?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a lot of firing there, given the fact that at Dubac and above Dubac there's a quarry with 120-millimetre mortars positioned there, rocket launchers as well, 120-millimetre guns, and there was heavy firing there. Four of the mortars, rocket launchers, were captured, and two of the guns, the 120-millimetre guns as well as two Maljutka rocket launchers.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Four mortars, two Maljutka rocket launchers, and two guns were captured on that occasion. These were captured from Croatian paramilitary units, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from Croatian paramilitary units. I know that those mortars were later taken to Titograd. I asked to leave them there, where they were, but my request was not met.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What about the Croatian units? If they had this kind of artillery in those positions, did they use this artillery power to put up resistance? How long did that last and how long had they been in that position for prior to that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They fired from those positions continually, as our units were between Cavtat, meaning Zvekovica, Mlini and Srebreno as for my units units. They were firing from that area. Also along the operational axis of the 3rd and 4th Battalions, they operated in the direction of Ivanica, Uskoplje, Gornji Brgat, Donji Brgat, Obod, and then down the road to Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me if your artillery from the 9th Military Naval Sector ever fired on Zarkovica, Srdj, or Bosanka.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not in that period of time. At that time, the main focus of our operations was on Dubac, Brgat, Gornji Brgat, Donji Brgat, that was taken then, yes. And Zarkovica as well, as well as the general area around the Belvedere Hotel that was fortified.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And when did your artillery fire on Srdj and Bosanka? When was that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was much later, in November. On the 26th of October, the 130-millimetre battery that I had was withdrawn towards the Radovici barracks. And the 85-millimetre battery was returned to Prevlaka for maintenance of its targeting equipment -- of its sighting equipment. I reckoned that I would not need any artillery at that time, because we had already got very close to the town of Dubrovnik itself. And we received no further orders for operations to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You say that this was on the 26th of October?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what about this artillery, was any of it returned to these positions facing Dubrovnik after the 26th?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the month of November, I think, sometime around the 8th or 10th. The 130-millimetre battery returned to the area of Cilipi airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What about the 85-millimetre guns? After they were sighted, then what happened?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they were brought, too, but I'm not sure. I'm not sure of whether they were used, but they were probably in the area. These were poor artillery pieces. Technically, they were not in very good shape.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Can you just be more precise concerning the characteristics. These artillery pieces you refer to, what does this actually refer to?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I was saying, the 85-millimetre battery was technically in poor condition. The cannons were faulty. They were -- they had even been decommissioned previously, and we hardly ever used them, only for training purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on page 57, between lines 2 and 5, I do not see in the interpretation that these were cannons that were faulty to a large degree. I do not see that in the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It does appear later at 57, lines 10, 11, 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the problem here is we have to deal with very specific artillery vocabulary here. So faulty to a large degree is not the right translation for "veliko rasturanje." Perhaps the witness can explain exactly what this means. This is very important and it is highly relevant. This should be explained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'll try to deal with it. I'll try to clarify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, could you please explain for the transcript, so that it would properly reflect everything that was said, could you give the characteristics of these 85-millimetre cannons that you talked about.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because they were used to a very large extent, these -- these cannons were obsolete and we were even decommissioned in the military naval sector and district. For their sighting equipment -- because of their sighting equipment, which had to be readjusted all the time. And also because of the barrels themselves. When there was firing from these barrels, there was dissipation. So these cannons were not used. This battery was not used for targets that included several points, and we hardly ever used them. I don't know the exact date, but it is a fact that both of these batteries were resubordinated to the commander of the 2nd Tactical Group. I found them under his subordination when I came to the theatre. Because, as far as my narrow zone is concerned, where my territorial units operated, from the sea to the road between Herceg-Novi and Dubrovnik, there were no artillery targets all the way to Cavtat. And in Cavtat, there was no fighting. So for taking these villages, we did not even use the artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, until when was this artillery in the 2nd Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not know the exact date, but I think that on the 21st of October the 2nd Tactical Group was disbanded. Then certainly -- or perhaps two or three days before that, these batteries were returned to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to ask you, and you are an expert in these matters, could you explain to the Trial Chamber and all of us, when you say: Greater dissipation or dispersion when barrels are used and when cannons are fired, can you explain this to us. Can you explain it lay terms, what this actually means so that we would understand.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The shells of a battery or the hits of a battery fall within an ellipse of about 100 metres of width and let us say the length is about 50 metres. It depends on the distance. It depends on the volley. If this ellipse is larger -- or rather, if the hits miss, either in terms of direction or width, if these distances are not -- are too big, then this is unacceptably imprecise, these volleys are unacceptably imprecise. So then the barrels are changed and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This was a very graphic explanation, and this ellipsis you refer to now was clear. So when you say that there is greater dissipation of these volleys, how much dispersion is there when you're talking about a greater dispersion? What is the range that we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I am not an artillery man myself. I'm a naval man, a rocket man. But I did learn this. I think that we can look at it this way. If the distances are 20 to 50 per cent larger, if the margin of error is that big, then there has to be a correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I did not understand this. When you said if the distances are 20 to 50 per cent bigger.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to the ellipsis. If the ellipsis is there and it -- and if it is 20 to 50 per cent bigger than it's supposed to be, then something has to be done in order to decrease it, either by way of sighting equipment or cannons or other parts of the cannon or the battery.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Correct me if I'm wrong, but if I understood you correctly within the dimensions of an ellipsis, if during dispersion the dimensions go up by 20 to 50 per cent, then this is this too great dispersion. And then sighting has to be readjusted on these cannons. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's more or less along those lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time, Mr. Rodic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, tell me, please, on the 5th of December, 1991, at that meeting with the Croatian ministers, when you were discussing the cease-fire in Cavtat, was it agreed on that occasion that the Croatian side would accept a surrender of weapons and an exit out of town by the volunteers?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not what was agreed upon then. We gave up on that particular request.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please have the assistance of the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Have you seen this document?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is this your interview that was published in the weekly of Nin on the 15th of November, 2001?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: If you look at page 1 of the document in the Serbian language version, is it correct that there is a number there, 04-AM/JM, two signatures, and on the right-hand side the date, the 5th of July, 2002. Is that what it says in the corner?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is any of the signatures on this document yours?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And who is the second person who signed this document?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whose signature this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was there anybody else with you then when you signed this?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably the investigator, but I don't know. I don't know who it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: On the 5th of July, 2002, did you give an interview to the investigators?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you give them this document or did they show it to you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they showed it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: During the interview, did you have anything specific to say regarding this document?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: On page 3 of the Serbian version, there is a picture, and I can recognise you. Tell me, this other man with the moustache, is that Dusan Mihajlovic, Minister of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia at that time, of course?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, in this particular paragraph in the Serbian version, to the left of the picture, there is a sentence that I am going to read out: "The most serious case of operations around Dubrovnik was on the 6th of December. On the 5th of December, I took part in negotiations" -- I'm sorry. May I just note that this is on page 5 of the English translation, the last paragraph. So I am going to repeat. "On the 5th of December, I was involved in negotiations with people from Dubrovnik. And in Cavtat, we agreed that there would be a halt to fighting, that they would accept to surrender their arms, and the volunteers would leave town. Three Croatian ministers participated in the negotiations. I remember the minister of maritime affairs, Davorin Rudolf, who told me that Croatia could not tolerate two major defeats, the fall of Dubrovnik after the fall of Vukovar, which was taken on the 18th of November. And on the 6th of December, a truce was supposed to come into force at 12.00." Is it correct that in this interview you say that they accepted the surrender of weapons and the volunteers leaving town?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says. That's what's written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you explain the difference to me, the difference between this statement -- or rather, this what you said in the interview to Nin and also the answer that you gave to my question a few minutes ago that these things were not agreed upon.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not say that they were not agreed upon. I said that we -- or rather, I gave up on these two particular items -- or rather, three items, volunteers, weapons, and returning to the situation of the 1st of October regarding the number of MUP members in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The next thing I'm going to ask you is on page 6 of the English version, the one but last paragraph. The one but last question. And in the Serbian version it's right beneath the photograph. A question was put, and I am going to read the second paragraph of the answer in the Serbian version, your answer to that question. So the question was: "Was the JNA's task to take Dubrovnik? It was said and written that the plan was to take both Dubrovnik and the territory as far as the Neretva River, which were to remain in Yugoslavia." That was the journalist's question. And in the second paragraph of your answer, that's the part that I'm interested in, you say: "I never saw, and even now I could not find the initial command in the Dubrovnik operation. But I think that the only objective was to take Srdj. That's what my chief of staff, Milan Zec, told me, but he also said that this had been abandoned."

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't know where this is. I couldn't find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Underneath your picture in the middle, your picture -- you and Mihajlovic together in this picture.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So now there are two paragraphs in your answer, and now I read out the last -- the second, actually, paragraph of that answer.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I don't understand your question. What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: My question is: When was it that Zec told you that, that the only objective of the Dubrovnik operation was to take Srdj?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's not the way it was, the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: That was my understanding on the basis of your answer.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did not revise this text. I could not have revised it. The substance of this text and all the answers I gave to the questions is fine, but some parts are very imprecise. I saw this text of course much later, considerably after its publication. In fact, if we're dealing about the objective to take control of Srdj, I wanted to say that while we were analysing the text of the directive itself, in the directive that we analysed, which I don't think is the right one because there's another one. Now, in that second directive it says: "Take control of Srdj." But of course that can't be the only objective; that is quite clear, clear to everyone, every soldier, not only commanders but all soldiers are aware of that. This is a very free interpretation and goes as far as being incorrect and does not correspond to how things stood.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Have I understood you correctly then that the paragraph that I read out, which is your response to the question from the journalist, is a very free interpretation on the part of that journalist?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Going as far as being completely incorrect?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Now, what about the next paragraph? I'm going to read that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And it is on page 7 of the English version, paragraph 3 from the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, it is the next column, next to the one we've just read out from, paragraph 2 from the top in the Serbian version it says: "The Admiral again approached the military archives. This time they allowed him to read the documents, but he was not allowed to take a single scrap of paper or make any photocopies." Could you tell me, please, whether that's true.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you provide the Prosecution with any documents?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't give any documents out from the archives, just what I received from certain officers with whom I had conversations to inform me before I went to The Hague, when I looked into the matter to see how the shelling of Dubrovnik came about and in preparation for my defence later on. But I didn't extract a single document from the archives. I couldn't do that, nor did I do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, please, whether you gave any military document to the representatives of the OTP during your conversations?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those I received from officers that I talked to and who had those documents with them, on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what documents those were, then.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were documents from the Dubrovnik operation. I don't know exactly which ones, but they were a set of documents, perhaps five or six of them. And then some of my own statements, my interviews, while I was the minister and later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What else did you provide them with?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what you mean. If you remind me, I'll be able to tell you. I don't know which you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Well, if you remember during the examination-in-chief, a number of documents were dealt with and tendered into evidence as Prosecution exhibits. Now, among those documents, if you remember, are there any you gave to the representatives of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I gave them several documents which I myself had received from the officers that I talked to, to provide me with information. They were my own officers or officers belonging to the 2nd Operational Group with whom I talked.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me who gave you those documents in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I should.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know why they enjoy -- whether they enjoy any protection, whether it's confidential, and whether it would be in their own interests for me to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you give to the representatives of the OTP a JNA map on which it said "national defence state secret?"

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Well, did you ask anybody for permission to do so, whether you were permitted to hand over documents of that nature?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the officer who -- in whose possession those maps were and who drew up the maps, I don't know how he came by the maps to begin with. He was given permission I think by the command of the 2nd Operational Group to keep those documents, and that included the maps. That's the explanation he gave me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Who gave you that explanation?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The officer from the command of the 2nd Operational Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Which officer? Can you give us his name?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've just said that it's not my duty to state his name, unless we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: May I ask -- would you please answer my question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, objection. The witness has indicated he would feel more comfortable giving a full answer if it were in private session. And perhaps if I can convey that through an objection, I would do that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you have any objection to private session, Mr. Rodic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do have an objection for us to go into private session for a response to my question, in view of the fact that all the documents that we're discussing and the ones that I'm asking questions about here were exhibits that were tendered as Prosecution Exhibits, and this was done at -- or in open session, which means that they were accessible to everybody, everybody could see them outside this courtroom. So that is the basic gist of my objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is not the crux of the issue with the witness. He's made it clear, from our perspective, that the names are what is of concern to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And the relevance of that, Ms. Somers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If the witness is concerned about perhaps putting certain persons at risk then -- and yet the Chamber would find the information relevant and helpful, then perhaps private session would be more appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is the view of the Chamber that if you wish to persist to get an answer, Mr. Rodic, we will go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in that case and in view of the grounds for my objection, I'll withdraw that. I don't think that anything is challenged or contested. But if that is your ruling, then I will give up on that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, did you personally have any documents of your own in your possession, that is, which you handed over to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not from the Dubrovnik operation. As far as official documents are concerned, I didn't have a single one. What I did have was several while I was a minister in the Serbian government. And then some extracts and excerpts from newspapers, some provisions which touched upon the problems they were interested in. But as far as official documents are concerned, I did not have a single one. When I retired, all my notebooks, working notebooks, wartime notebooks and diaries, were taken away. So I was left without a single scrap of paper which would help me refresh my memory of those days and events.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me who confiscated those documents?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The security service.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were you detained, taken into custody, arrested?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Well, how then were they able to take these documents away from you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did so when I handed over my duties. I had to leave all my notebooks behind on the table, on my desk. I wasn't allowed to take any papers or documents with me. That's how they did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was that in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's right, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You said a moment ago in response to question from me linked to that portion of the interview which you gave to the weekly magazine Nin that you did have a chance to read through the documents in the archives, but that you were not permitted to take out any document or to make any photocopies. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So that means that from the archives you reviewed those documents in, you -- did you just review those documents, or did your lawyers do so, too?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I left for The Hague, I took a look at them myself. And after my return, a long time afterwards, maybe half a year later, we were given permission to access those -- the documents, but not to take them out or to photocopy them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you look at -- review the documents yourself, only you, or your lawyers as well?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said my lawyers, too. My lawyers and myself. They spent more time reviewing them and two investigators as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And you claim that you did not take a single document out for use from that archive?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. Towards the end, if you want to have full information about this --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I be allowed to give an explanation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We asked, on the basis to access to military archives, for them to photocopy -- provide photocopies of about 600 documents for us. However, I was already due to go to The Hague to declare myself, to plead. And when we were provided with 60 documents, I think, approximately 60 documents, of which 50 per cent were such poor photocopies - perhaps this was intentionally done - that they were absolutely illegible. So from these documents, what you're asking me about was probably one of those documents, which are in possession of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you gave the Prosecution these 60 documents?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't give them anything. All I'm saying is that my lawyers were given 60 documents, 50 per cent of which were useless because they were poor photocopies and illegible. And all I'm saying is probably they were forwarded to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Well, did your lawyers provide the OTP with these documents?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know what the procedure is. They told me that if the Prosecution provided with any documents, then the Defence teams should be, too. They must be disclosed to both parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The interviews you mentioned having handed over to the OTP, do you mean by that the interviews that you granted to newspapers and that appeared in newspaper articles?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many such interviews you handed over to the Prosecution, because I assume these are your own personal documents?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. But -- well, perhaps two or three interviews. One was from the ministry, and I think the other two were given while I was the commander -- or rather, immediately after I retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And that doesn't include the Nin interview that you have before you now, does it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. This interview -- they gave me this copy, this interview. And I was a little surprised and taken aback. And we discussed some of the incorrect points. And I said that I did not review the text or redact it, but that I was in The Hague and that there were certain things that were incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: That means that in the interview with the Prosecution, you answered their questions in detail with respect to this interview that appeared in the weekly magazine Nin?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how detailed it was, but yes, they did ask me what they were interested in learning. I can't say. We didn't go item by item. We just discussed the questions that they were interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I should now like to ask you to look at page 1 of the B/C/S version, which is in English page 3. The last paragraph on that page, and there's a question and answer there. Page 3 for the English, and page 1 in the B/C/S. It is the last paragraph, and you were asked the following: "The military units under your command, were they military units or did they include territorials and paramilitaries?" And then on the next page it says: "Were militaries under your command or were territorials and paramilitary formations also there?" I read that out and then on the next page under your photograph you begin your answer. You say: "We didn't have any paramilitary formations. There were Yugoslav People's Army units there, which were reinforced with reserve forces. And we also had territorial units. They were companies mobilised by the Montenegrin Territorial Defence staff." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It's a bit inaccurate. JNA units reinforced with reserve forces, because the JNA units already include some of the reserve forces, but with the exception of that particular bit, everything else is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The title of the interview, the heading, is it correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Therefore, this is not a question of a liberal interpretation by the journalist? That's what you stated, the journalist. I'm not guilty.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I certainly wasn't the one who told him to give this title to the interview. It was part of the interview that I said that I believed I wasn't guilty.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, can we have this tendered into evidence as a Defence exhibit and be assigned an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is marked D45.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, correct me if I'm wrong about the date. But in October 2001, an indictment was made public against you, General Strugar, Vladimir Kovacevic, and Milan Zec, after which you surrendered to The Hague Tribunal of your own free will in November of 2001. I believe it was in February 2002 that you were provisionally released. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it true that on the 27th of August, 2003, you faced a Trial Chamber of the Tribunal, and you pleaded guilty on all counts, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me more about the period between October 2001 and the 27th of August, 2003. Were you preparing your defence, given the fact that you had pleaded not guilty in that period of time?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was preparing my defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: As you went about preparing your defence, you reviewed all the documents that you were given by the OTP, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you read specifically all the witness statements that the OTP disclosed to you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: While preparing your defence, did you talk to any witnesses who were to testify on your behalf? I'm talking about that particular period of time.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked to quite a number of officers who would then inform me about those developments in a proper way, because they themselves had taken part. And those were potential witnesses, too. But I did not specifically ask anyone to appear as a witness or to give an official statement to me or to any of my investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The witnesses you interviewed, were those mostly officers from the 9th VPS, the sector under your command between October and December 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you also talk to officers who were members of your staff at the time, in the 9th VPS?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did talk to some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were some of those officers from the command of the 2nd Operational Group?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, some who lived in Belgrade, some who were retired, some of those I saw of those who came to talk to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So the documents you handed over to the OTP were documents that you originally received from those potential witnesses, the officers that you spoke to. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Those were no potential witnesses. They declared they did not wish to be considered as potential witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When they talked to you, did they at least tell you that they wished to assist you with your defence and that they were therefore handing material over to you that was in their possession?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What about the maps that were handed over to the OTP and that were tendered into evidence during the examination-in-chief? What about those maps? Did they, too, come from the same officers that you spoke to?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me or confirm with any degree of certainty that those maps are fully accurate or authentic, should I say, with an accurate representation of all the markings that the maps bear?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so, as far as their authenticity is concerned. There are some inaccuracies [Realtime transcript read in error "accuracies"], though, because the maps were not properly drawn by those who were in charge of that, with the command of the 2nd Operational Group. But those are no material inaccuracies. I believe the maps are authentic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Are those the original maps?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are maps that were copied. Copies were made based on the originals.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. There's a mistake of consequence in the transcript, page 75, line 17. The witness said: "There are some inaccuracies," and it has been shown as "accuracies."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may -- if I may just be allowed to say a couple of words about the maps. When I went through the archive, the files, I established that in addition to my own documents, my combat orders, my orders, my reports, there wasn't a single map, a single working map, for any of my decisions or maps that were part of any of my orders, which struck me as really strange. You have an entire archive, all the files, and not a single map from the commander of one of the naval sectors. That was the main reason I was surprised that someone had taken those away. The main reason was for me to get another map that talked about the way that the Dubrovnik operation was run. That was the reason behind it. That was my main motive. And in terms of myself preparing my defence, I think I was perfectly within my rights to do that. Even now I can't tell you where those maps of the commander of the 9th Sector are.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, when you said redrawn or modified, for the benefit of the interpretation and transcript please let us clarify. Are these copied maps any different from photocopied maps? And if so, how?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are no differences, no discrepancies. They are completely identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In terms of the technical procedure, that's what I want to know. The maps that you handed over to the OTP, are those photocopies or one map was used to copy markings on to a different map, from that original map I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a case of the latter. Details were copied from the original map, the marks made on the original map. Those were not photocopied.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I would have to object. There was a word put in the mouth of the witness. Page 76, line 18. Mr. Jokic, when you said "redrawn or modified," we checked the record and other than the use once of the word "modified," it doesn't appear that the witness ever used that term.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you allow. Again, this is a problem with the transcript. The witness keeps talking about redrawn maps, and we have the word "copy" here. He keeps saying "redrawn," but the interpretation you are receiving is copied. Therefore, in this last situation that my learned friend and colleague is talking about, the word that is actually being used is "redrawn," although the word in the transcript is "copied," if I'm not mistaken. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: My objection is to either the use of the word modified in the words of the witness which does not appear on the record by Mr. Rodic, as if quoting from the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think we will proceed on the basis that the evidence of this witness in this respect was that the map was redrawn, full stop. And if you could proceed from there, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. I merely wanted to use these questions to explain the difference between a map that is copied and a map that is redrawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, were you the one who did the redrawing from the original map on to a new map?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made sure that every map that was drawn was faithful to the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So who did the actual redrawing?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who know how to do it, officers that were in charge of that sort of task their whole lives while they were still in active service.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Are these the officers that were willing to assist you in preparing your defence?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Those weren't the same officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that you took the maps to be redrawn by officers with whom you never ever discussed the subject of your defence?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were friends, officers who were friends, and who took no part in the Dubrovnik operation, but by the very nature of their job they know how to make maps. They are qualified for that in every way.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What then are the names of those officers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. The witness has indicated earlier he does not care to deal in giving out names of persons, unless it's in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe we're dealing with a technical matter here, because that's what redrawing these maps means. It's a purely technical procedure. I see no reason to go into private session, but obviously it's up to you to decide.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe it's all part of the same issue of persons who may or may not -- for whose security the witness is concerned and I believe it has no difference than the earlier grounds for objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you able to indicate your position on this, Mr. Jokic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am reluctant to give the names of those persons. They are not in any way involved in terms of knowing anything else about the subject. The only thing those people are qualified for is to draw. Considering the risk, the considerable risk, at which they might be put and having in mind the fact that these maps are confidential -- or they were classified at the time, I am not willing to disclose the names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber takes the same position as before, Mr. Rodic. If you insist on an answer, we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall move on, in that case, Your Honour. We have several questions left. I'll just leave this out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I doubt if you've got time for several questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two questions, Your Honour. Two questions. I believe we'll have sufficient time for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, how then are we to believe in the accuracy of those maps? They are not the original maps. These were maps that were redrawn.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I believe these maps are faithful to the original, and I stand by that opinion. I'm not sure if there is another way at all for me to convince you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Very well then. Just another question. By way of clarification you said that those maps used to be classified but no longer are. What I want to know is what your position is in that matter. Can you please elucidate. Are these maps classified or not?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe the degree of confidentiality 14 years later - and we are talking about an operation that was run by an army that is no longer around in a state that is no longer around - after all those developments, this one state ceased to exist and a wholly new state was created, or rather, two new states. I think this concept of something being classified or confidential is so academic that we could do better than to treat it with a certain degree of liberty.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it your view then that if this is no longer classified, you still refuse to give the names of the people who informed you about this and who helped you with this, or will you now agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you misunderstood me --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. The witness never refused. The witness he would do so, if in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We fully understand the position. You were saying something, Admiral.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. What I wish to say is the following: Prior to my arrival in The Hague, I requested to inspect my combat documents. The head of the archive, Colonel Prsic, I believe I can say his name now because this person has retired and I don't think there is any substantial risk involved. He told me that that was highly classified material and that I would not be allowed to inspect that material. I said, "Well, these are documents I made myself and I signed." This is a tactical document that talks about combat that went on 12 years ago, so why on earth would I not be allowed to see it? He said, "These are the rules. These are the rules of filing and this is how the archive is used." And that's why I am giving you my pragmatic position on these documents in general, documents that may prove helpful in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am finished for the day, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will adjourn then for the weekend and resume on Monday morning.
